1	---
2	title: Transactions and batch queries
3	description: This page explains the transactions API of Prisma Client
4	url: /orm/v7/prisma-client/queries/transactions
5	metaTitle: Transactions and batch queries (Reference)
6	metaDescription: This page explains the transactions API of Prisma Client.
7	---
8	
9	A database transaction is a sequence of read/write operations guaranteed to succeed or fail as a whole (ACID properties: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable).
10	
11	Prisma Client supports transactions in several ways:
12	
13	| Scenario            | Technique                                |
14	| :------------------ | :--------------------------------------- |
15	| Dependent writes    | Nested writes                            |
16	| Independent writes  | `$transaction([])` API, Batch operations |
17	| Read, modify, write | Interactive transactions                 |
18	
19	## Nested writes
20	
21	A [nested write](/orm/v7/prisma-client/queries/relation-queries#nested-writes) performs multiple operations on related records in a single transaction:
22	
23	```ts
24	// Create user with posts in a single transaction
25	const user = await prisma.user.create({
26	  data: {
27	    email: "alice@prisma.io",
28	    posts: {
29	      create: [{ title: "Post 1" }, { title: "Post 2" }],
30	    },
31	  },
32	});
33	```
34	
35	## Batch operations
36	
37	These bulk operations run as transactions:
38	
39	- `createMany()` / `createManyAndReturn()`
40	- `updateMany()` / `updateManyAndReturn()`
41	- `deleteMany()`
42	
43	## The `$transaction` API
44	
45	### Sequential operations
46	
47	Pass an array of queries to execute sequentially in a transaction:
48	
49	```ts
50	const [posts, totalPosts] = await prisma.$transaction([
51	  prisma.post.findMany({ where: { title: { contains: "prisma" } } }),
52	  prisma.post.count(),
53	]);
54	```
55	
56	With options:
57	
58	```ts
59	await prisma.$transaction(
60	  [prisma.resource.deleteMany({ where: { name: "name" } }), prisma.resource.createMany({ data })],
61	  { isolationLevel: Prisma.TransactionIsolationLevel.Serializable },
62	);
63	```
64	
65	### Interactive transactions
66	
67	For complex logic between queries, use interactive transactions:
68	
69	```ts
70	const result = await prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
71	  const sender = await tx.account.update({
72	    data: { balance: { decrement: 100 } },
73	    where: { email: "alice@prisma.io" },
74	  });
75	
76	  if (sender.balance < 0) {
77	    throw new Error("Insufficient funds");
78	  }
79	
80	  return await tx.account.update({
81	    data: { balance: { increment: 100 } },
82	    where: { email: "bob@prisma.io" },
83	  });
84	});
85	```
86	
87	:::warning
88	Keep transactions short. Long-running transactions hurt performance and can cause deadlocks.
89	:::
90	
91	**Options:**
92	
93	```ts
94	await prisma.$transaction(
95	  async (tx) => {
96	    /* ... */
97	  },
98	  {
99	    maxWait: 5000, // Max wait to acquire transaction (default: 2000ms)
100	    timeout: 10000, // Max transaction run time (default: 5000ms)
101	    isolationLevel: Prisma.TransactionIsolationLevel.Serializable,
102	  },
103	);
104	```
105	
106	### Transaction isolation level
107	
108	:::info
109	
110	This feature is not available on MongoDB, because MongoDB does not support isolation levels.
111	
112	:::
113	
114	You can set the transaction [isolation level](https://www.prisma.io/dataguide/intro/database-glossary#isolation-levels) for transactions.
115	
116	#### Set the isolation level
117	
118	To set the transaction isolation level, use the `isolationLevel` option in the second parameter of the API.
119	
120	For sequential operations:
121	
122	```ts
123	await prisma.$transaction(
124	  [
125	    // Prisma Client operations running in a transaction...
126	  ],
127	  {
128	    isolationLevel: Prisma.TransactionIsolationLevel.Serializable, // optional, default defined by database configuration
129	  },
130	);
131	```
132	
133	For an interactive transaction:
134	
135	```jsx
136	await prisma.$transaction(
137	  async (prisma) => {
138	    // Code running in a transaction...
139	  },
140	  {
141	    isolationLevel: Prisma.TransactionIsolationLevel.Serializable, // optional, default defined by database configuration
142	    maxWait: 5000, // default: 2000
143	    timeout: 10000, // default: 5000
144	  },
145	);
146	```
147	
148	#### Supported isolation levels
149	
150	Prisma Client supports the following isolation levels if they are available in the underlying database:
151	
152	- `ReadUncommitted`
153	- `ReadCommitted`
154	- `RepeatableRead`
155	- `Snapshot`
156	- `Serializable`
157	
158	The isolation levels available for each database connector are as follows:
159	
160	| Database    | `ReadUncommitted` | `ReadCommitted` | `RepeatableRead` | `Snapshot` | `Serializable` |
161	| ----------- | ----------------- | --------------- | ---------------- | ---------- | -------------- |
162	| PostgreSQL  | ✔️                | ✔️              | ✔️               | No         | ✔️             |
163	| MySQL       | ✔️                | ✔️              | ✔️               | No         | ✔️             |
164	| SQL Server  | ✔️                | ✔️              | ✔️               | ✔️         | ✔️             |
165	| CockroachDB | No                | No              | No               | No         | ✔️             |
166	| SQLite      | No                | No              | No               | No         | ✔️             |
167	
168	By default, Prisma Client sets the isolation level to the value currently configured in your database.
169	
170	The isolation levels configured by default in each database are as follows:
171	
172	| Database    | Default          |
173	| ----------- | ---------------- |
174	| PostgreSQL  | `ReadCommitted`  |
175	| MySQL       | `RepeatableRead` |
176	| SQL Server  | `ReadCommitted`  |
177	| CockroachDB | `Serializable`   |
178	| SQLite      | `Serializable`   |
179	
180	#### Database-specific information on isolation levels
181	
182	See the following resources:
183	
184	- [Transaction isolation levels in PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.3/runtime-config-client.html#GUC-DEFAULT-TRANSACTION-ISOLATION)
185	- [Transaction isolation levels in Microsoft SQL Server](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/set-transaction-isolation-level-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver15)
186	- [Transaction isolation levels in MySQL](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-transaction-isolation-levels.html)
187	
188	CockroachDB and SQLite only support the `Serializable` isolation level.
189	
190	### Transaction timing issues
191	
192	:::info
193	
194	- The solution in this section does not apply to MongoDB, because MongoDB does not support [isolation levels](https://www.prisma.io/dataguide/intro/database-glossary#isolation-levels).
195	- The timing issues discussed in this section do not apply to CockroachDB and SQLite, because these databases only support the highest `Serializable` isolation level.
196	
197	:::
198	
199	When two or more transactions run concurrently in certain [isolation levels](https://www.prisma.io/dataguide/intro/database-glossary#isolation-levels), timing issues can cause write conflicts or deadlocks, such as the violation of unique constraints. For example, consider the following sequence of events where Transaction A and Transaction B both attempt to execute a `deleteMany` and a `createMany` operation:
200	
201	1. Transaction B: `createMany` operation creates a new set of rows.
202	1. Transaction B: The application commits transaction B.
203	1. Transaction A: `createMany` operation.
204	1. Transaction A: The application commits transaction A. The new rows conflict with the rows that transaction B added at step 2.
205	
206	This conflict can occur at the isolation level `ReadCommitted`, which is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL and Microsoft SQL Server. To avoid this problem, you can set a higher isolation level (`RepeatableRead` or `Serializable`). You can set the isolation level on a transaction. This overrides your database isolation level for that transaction.
207	
208	To avoid transaction write conflicts and deadlocks on a transaction:
209	
210	1. On your transaction, use the `isolationLevel` parameter to `Prisma.TransactionIsolationLevel.Serializable`.
211	
212	   This ensures that your application commits multiple concurrent or parallel transactions as if they were run serially. When a transaction fails due to a write conflict or deadlock, Prisma Client returns a [P2034 error](/orm/v7/reference/error-reference#p2034).
213	
214	2. In your application code, add a retry around your transaction to handle any P2034 errors, as shown in this example:
215	
216	   ```ts
217	   import { Prisma, PrismaClient } from "../prisma/generated/client";
218	
219	   const prisma = new PrismaClient();
220	   async function main() {
221	     const MAX_RETRIES = 5;
222	     let retries = 0;
223	
224	     let result;
225	     while (retries < MAX_RETRIES) {
226	       try {
227	         result = await prisma.$transaction(
228	           [
229	             prisma.user.deleteMany({
230	               where: {
231	                 /** args */
232	               },
233	             }),
234	             prisma.post.createMany({
235	               data: {
236	                 /** args */
237	               },
238	             }),
239	           ],
240	           {
241	             isolationLevel: Prisma.TransactionIsolationLevel.Serializable,
242	           },
243	         );
244	         break;
245	       } catch (error) {
246	         if (error.code === "P2034") {
247	           retries++;
248	           continue;
249	         }
250	         throw error;
251	       }
252	     }
253	   }
254	   ```
255	
256	### Using `$transaction` within `Promise.all()`
257	
258	If you wrap a `$transaction` inside a call to `Promise.all()`, the queries inside the transaction will be executed _serially_ (i.e. one after another):
259	
260	```ts
261	await prisma.$transaction(async (prisma) => {
262	  await Promise.all([
263	    prisma.user.findMany(),
264	    prisma.user.findMany(),
265	    prisma.user.findMany(),
266	    prisma.user.findMany(),
267	    prisma.user.findMany(),
268	    prisma.user.findMany(),
269	    prisma.user.findMany(),
270	    prisma.user.findMany(),
271	    prisma.user.findMany(),
272	    prisma.user.findMany(),
273	  ]);
274	});
275	```
276	
277	This may be counterintuitive because `Promise.all()` usually _parallelizes_ the calls passed into it.
278	
279	The reason for this behaviour is that:
280	
281	- One transaction means that all queries inside it have to be run on the same connection.
282	- A database connection can only ever execute one query at a time.
283	- As one query blocks the connection while it is doing its work, putting a transaction into `Promise.all` effectively means that queries should be ran one after another.
284	
285	## Dependent writes
286	
287	Writes are **dependent** when operations rely on the result of a preceding operation (e.g., using a database-generated ID).
288	
289	### Nested writes for dependent operations
290	
291	Use nested writes when you need to create related records atomically:
292	
293	```ts
294	const team = await prisma.team.create({
295	  data: {
296	    name: "Aurora Adventures",
297	    members: {
298	      create: { email: "alice@prisma.io" },
299	    },
300	  },
301	});
302	```
303	
304	If any operation fails, Prisma Client rolls back the entire transaction.
305	
306	:::note
307	The `$transaction([])` API cannot pass IDs between operations - use nested writes when you need the generated ID from one record to create another.
308	:::
309	
310	## Independent writes
311	
312	Writes are **independent** if they don't rely on the result of a previous operation. Use these for:
313	
314	- Updating the status of multiple orders to "Dispatched"
315	- Marking a list of emails as "Read"
316	
317	### Bulk operations
318	
319	```ts
320	const updateUsers = await prisma.user.updateMany({
321	  where: { email: { contains: "prisma.io" } },
322	  data: { role: "ADMIN" },
323	});
324	```
325	
326	### Using `$transaction([])` for independent writes
327	
328	```ts
329	const [deleteResult, createResult] = await prisma.$transaction([
330	  prisma.post.deleteMany({ where: { authorId: 7 } }),
331	  prisma.user.delete({ where: { id: 7 } }),
332	]);
333	```
334	
335	### Scenario: Pre-computed IDs and the `$transaction([])` API
336	
337	If you pre-compute IDs (e.g., using UUIDs), you can use either nested writes or `$transaction([])` since both operations know the ID upfront.
338	
339	#### When to use bulk operations
340	
341	Consider bulk operations as a solution if:
342	
343	- ✔ You want to update a batch of the _same type_ of record, like a batch of emails
344	
345	#### Scenario: Marking emails as read
346	
347	You are building a service like gmail.com, and your customer wants a **"Mark as read"** feature that allows users to mark all emails as read. Each update to the status of an email is an independent write because the emails do not depend on one another - for example, the "Happy Birthday! 🍰" email from your aunt is unrelated to the promotional email from IKEA.
348	
349	In the following schema, a `User` can have many received emails (a one-to-many relationship):
350	
351	```ts
352	model User {
353	  id    Int       @id @default(autoincrement())
354	  email           String @unique
355	  receivedEmails  Email[] // Many emails
356	}
357	
358	model Email {
359	  id      Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
360	  user    User    @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
361	  userId  Int
362	  subject String
363	  body    String
364	  unread  Boolean
365	}
366	```
367	
368	Based on this schema, you can use `updateMany` to mark all unread emails as read:
369	
370	```ts
371	await prisma.email.updateMany({
372	  where: {
373	    user: {
374	      id: 10,
375	    },
376	    unread: true,
377	  },
378	  data: {
379	    unread: false,
380	  },
381	});
382	```
383	
384	#### Can I use nested writes with bulk operations?
385	
386	No - neither `updateMany` nor `deleteMany` currently supports nested writes. For example, you cannot delete multiple teams and all of their members (a cascading delete):
387	
388	```ts highlight=8;delete
389	await prisma.team.deleteMany({
390	  where: {
391	    id: {
392	      in: [2, 99, 2, 11],
393	    },
394	  },
395	  data: {
396	    members: {}, // Cannot access members here // [!code --]
397	  },
398	});
399	```
400	
401	#### Can I use bulk operations with the `$transaction([])` API?
402	
403	Yes — for example, you can include multiple `deleteMany` operations inside a `$transaction([])`.
404	
405	### `$transaction([])` API
406	
407	The `$transaction([])` API is generic solution to independent writes that allows you to run multiple operations as a single, atomic operation - if any operation fails, Prisma Client rolls back the entire transaction.
408	
409	Its also worth noting that operations are executed according to the order they are placed in the transaction.
410	
411	```ts
412	await prisma.$transaction([iRunFirst, iRunSecond, iRunThird]);
413	```
414	
415	> **Note**: Using a query in a transaction does not influence the order of operations in the query itself.
416	
417	As Prisma Client evolves, use cases for the `$transaction([])` API will increasingly be replaced by more specialized bulk operations (such as `createMany`) and nested writes.
418	
419	#### When to use the `$transaction([])` API
420	
421	Consider the `$transaction([])` API if:
422	
423	- ✔ You want to update a batch that includes different types of records, such as emails and users. The records do not need to be related in any way.
424	- ✔ You want to batch raw SQL queries (`$executeRaw`) - for example, for features that Prisma Client does not yet support.
425	
426	#### Scenario: Privacy legislation
427	
428	GDPR and other privacy legislation give users the right to request that an organization deletes all of their personal data. In the following example schema, a `User` can have many posts and private messages:
429	
430	```prisma
431	model User {
432	  id              Int              @id @default(autoincrement())
433	  posts           Post[]
434	  privateMessages PrivateMessage[]
435	}
436	
437	model Post {
438	  id      Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
439	  user    User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
440	  userId  Int
441	  title   String
442	  content String
443	}
444	
445	model PrivateMessage {
446	  id      Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
447	  user    User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
448	  userId  Int
449	  message String
450	}
451	```
452	
453	If a user invokes the right to be forgotten, we must delete three records: the user record, private messages, and posts. It is critical that _all_ delete operations succeed together or not at all, which makes this a use case for a transaction. However, using a single bulk operation like `deleteMany` is not possible in this scenario because we need to delete across three models. Instead, we can use the `$transaction([])` API to run three operations together - two `deleteMany` and one `delete`:
454	
455	```ts
456	const id = 9; // User to be deleted
457	
458	const deletePosts = prisma.post.deleteMany({
459	  where: {
460	    userId: id,
461	  },
462	});
463	
464	const deleteMessages = prisma.privateMessage.deleteMany({
465	  where: {
466	    userId: id,
467	  },
468	});
469	
470	const deleteUser = prisma.user.delete({
471	  where: {
472	    id: id,
473	  },
474	});
475	
476	await prisma.$transaction([deletePosts, deleteMessages, deleteUser]); // Operations succeed or fail together
477	```
478	
479	#### Scenario: Pre-computed IDs and the `$transaction([])` API
480	
481	Dependent writes are not supported by the `$transaction([])` API - if operation A relies on the ID generated by operation B, use [nested writes](#nested-writes). However, if you _pre-computed_ IDs (for example, by generating GUIDs), your writes become independent. Consider the sign-up flow from the nested writes example:
482	
483	```ts
484	await prisma.team.create({
485	  data: {
486	    name: "Aurora Adventures",
487	    members: {
488	      create: {
489	        email: "alice@prisma.io",
490	      },
491	    },
492	  },
493	});
494	```
495	
496	Instead of auto-generating IDs, change the `id` fields of `Team` and `User` to a `String` (if you do not provide a value, a UUID is generated automatically). This example uses UUIDs:
497	
498	```prisma highlight=2,9;delete|3,10;add
499	model Team {
500	  id      Int    @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code --]
501	  id      String @id @default(uuid()) // [!code ++]
502	  name    String
503	  members User[]
504	}
505	
506	model User {
507	  id    Int    @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code --]
508	  id    String @id @default(uuid()) // [!code ++]
509	  email String @unique
510	  teams Team[]
511	}
512	```
513	
514	Refactor the sign-up flow example to use the `$transaction([])` API instead of nested writes:
515	
516	```ts
517	import { v4 } from "uuid";
518	
519	const teamID = v4();
520	const userID = v4();
521	
522	await prisma.$transaction([
523	  prisma.user.create({
524	    data: {
525	      id: userID,
526	      email: "alice@prisma.io",
527	      team: {
528	        id: teamID,
529	      },
530	    },
531	  }),
532	  prisma.team.create({
533	    data: {
534	      id: teamID,
535	      name: "Aurora Adventures",
536	    },
537	  }),
538	]);
539	```
540	
541	Technically you can still use nested writes with pre-computed APIs if you prefer that syntax:
542	
543	```ts
544	import { v4 } from "uuid";
545	
546	const teamID = v4();
547	const userID = v4();
548	
549	await prisma.team.create({
550	  data: {
551	    id: teamID,
552	    name: "Aurora Adventures",
553	    members: {
554	      create: {
555	        id: userID,
556	        email: "alice@prisma.io",
557	        team: {
558	          id: teamID,
559	        },
560	      },
561	    },
562	  },
563	});
564	```
565	
566	There's no compelling reason to switch to manually generated IDs and the `$transaction([])` API if you are already using auto-generated IDs and nested writes.
567	
568	## Read, modify, write
569	
570	In some cases you may need to perform custom logic as part of an atomic operation - also known as the [read-modify-write pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Read%E2%80%93modify%E2%80%93write). The following is an example of the read-modify-write pattern:
571	
572	- Read a value from the database
573	- Run some logic to manipulate that value (for example, contacting an external API)
574	- Write the value back to the database
575	
576	All operations should **succeed or fail together** without making unwanted changes to the database, but you do not necessarily need to use an actual database transaction. This section of the guide describes two ways to work with Prisma Client and the read-modify-write pattern:
577	
578	- Designing idempotent APIs
579	- Optimistic concurrency control
580	
581	### Idempotent APIs
582	
583	Idempotency is the ability to run the same logic with the same parameters multiple times with the same result: the **effect on the database** is the same whether you run the logic once or one thousand times. For example:
584	
585	- **NOT IDEMPOTENT**: Upsert (update-or-insert) a user in the database with email address `"letoya@prisma.io"`. The `User` table **does not** enforce unique email addresses. The effect on the database is different if you run the logic once (one user created) or ten times (ten users created).
586	- **IDEMPOTENT**: Upsert (update-or-insert) a user in the database with the email address `"letoya@prisma.io"`. The `User` table **does** enforce unique email addresses. The effect on the database is the same if you run the logic once (one user created) or ten times (existing user is updated with the same input).
587	
588	Idempotency is something you can and should actively design into your application wherever possible.
589	
590	#### When to design an idempotent API
591	
592	- ✔ You need to be able to retry the same logic without creating unwanted side-effects in the databases
593	
594	#### Scenario: Upgrading a Slack team
595	
596	You are creating an upgrade flow for Slack that allows teams to unlock paid features. Teams can choose between different plans and pay per user, per month. You use Stripe as your payment gateway, and extend your `Team` model to store a `stripeCustomerId`. Subscriptions are managed in Stripe.
597	
598	```prisma highlight=5;normal
599	model Team {
600	  id               Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
601	  name             String
602	  User             User[]
603	  stripeCustomerId String? // [!code highlight]
604	}
605	```
606	
607	The upgrade flow looks like this:
608	
609	1. Count the number of users
610	2. Create a subscription in Stripe that includes the number of users
611	3. Associate the team with the Stripe customer ID to unlock paid features
612	
613	```ts
614	const teamId = 9;
615	const planId = "plan_id";
616	
617	// Count team members
618	const numTeammates = await prisma.user.count({
619	  where: {
620	    teams: {
621	      some: {
622	        id: teamId,
623	      },
624	    },
625	  },
626	});
627	
628	// Create a customer in Stripe for plan-9454549
629	const customer = await stripe.customers.create({
630	  externalId: teamId,
631	  plan: planId,
632	  quantity: numTeammates,
633	});
634	
635	// Update the team with the customer id to indicate that they are a customer
636	// and support querying this customer in Stripe from our application code.
637	await prisma.team.update({
638	  data: {
639	    customerId: customer.id,
640	  },
641	  where: {
642	    id: teamId,
643	  },
644	});
645	```
646	
647	This example has a problem: you can only run the logic _once_. Consider the following scenario:
648	
649	1. Stripe creates a new customer and subscription, and returns a customer ID
650	2. Updating the team **fails** - the team is not marked as a customer in the Slack database
651	3. The customer is charged by Stripe, but paid features are not unlocked in Slack because the team lacks a valid `customerId`
652	4. Running the same code again either:
653	   - Results in an error because the team (defined by `externalId`) already exists - Stripe never returns a customer ID
654	   - If `externalId` is not subject to a unique constraint, Stripe creates yet another subscription (**not idempotent**)
655	
656	You cannot re-run this code in case of an error and you cannot change to another plan without being charged twice.
657	
658	The following refactor (highlighted) introduces a mechanism that checks if a subscription already exists, and either creates the description or updates the existing subscription (which will remain unchanged if the input is identical):
659	
660	```ts highlight=12-27;normal
661	// Calculate the number of users times the cost per user
662	const numTeammates = await prisma.user.count({
663	  where: {
664	    teams: {
665	      some: {
666	        id: teamId,
667	      },
668	    },
669	  },
670	});
671	
672	// Find customer in Stripe // [!code highlight]
673	let customer = await stripe.customers.get({ externalId: teamID }); // [!code highlight]
674	
675	if (customer) {
676	  // [!code highlight]
677	  // If team already exists, update // [!code highlight]
678	  customer = await stripe.customers.update({
679	    // [!code highlight]
680	    externalId: teamId, // [!code highlight]
681	    plan: "plan_id", // [!code highlight]
682	    quantity: numTeammates, // [!code highlight]
683	  });
684	} else {
685	  customer = await stripe.customers.create({
686	    // If team does not exist, create customer
687	    externalId: teamId,
688	    plan: "plan_id",
689	    quantity: numTeammates,
690	  });
691	}
692	
693	// Update the team with the customer id to indicate that they are a customer
694	// and support querying this customer in Stripe from our application code.
695	await prisma.team.update({
696	  data: {
697	    customerId: customer.id,
698	  },
699	  where: {
700	    id: teamId,
701	  },
702	});
703	```
704	
705	You can now retry the same logic multiple times with the same input without adverse effect. To further enhance this example, you can introduce a mechanism whereby the subscription is cancelled or temporarily deactivated if the update does not succeed after a set number of attempts.
706	
707	### Optimistic concurrency control
708	
709	Optimistic concurrency control (OCC) is a model for handling concurrent operations on a single entity that does not rely on 🔒 locking. Instead, we **optimistically** assume that a record will remain unchanged in between reading and writing, and use a concurrency token (a timestamp or version field) to detect changes to a record.
710	
711	If a ❌ conflict occurs (someone else has changed the record since you read it), you cancel the transaction. Depending on your scenario, you can then:
712	
713	- Re-try the transaction (book another cinema seat)
714	- Throw an error (alert the user that they are about to overwrite changes made by someone else)
715	
716	This section describes how to build your own optimistic concurrency control. See also: Plans for [application-level optimistic concurrency control on GitHub](https://github.com/prisma/prisma/issues/4988)
717	
718	#### When to use optimistic concurrency control
719	
720	- ✔ You anticipate a high number of concurrent requests (multiple people booking cinema seats)
721	- ✔ You anticipate that conflicts between those concurrent requests will be rare
722	
723	Avoiding locks in an application with a high number of concurrent requests makes the application more resilient to load and more scalable overall. Although locking is not inherently bad, locking in a high concurrency environment can lead to unintended consequences - even if you are locking individual rows, and only for a short amount of time. For more information, see:
724	
725	- [Why ROWLOCK Hints Can Make Queries Slower and Blocking Worse in SQL Server](https://kendralittle.com/2016/02/04/why-rowlock-hints-can-make-queries-slower-and-blocking-worse-in-sql-server/)
726	
727	#### Scenario: Reserving a seat at the cinema
728	
729	You are creating a booking system for a cinema. Each movie has a set number of seats. The following schema models movies and seats:
730	
731	```ts
732	model Seat {
733	  id        Int   @id @default(autoincrement())
734	  userId    Int?
735	  claimedBy User? @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
736	  movieId   Int
737	  movie     Movie @relation(fields: [movieId], references: [id])
738	}
739	
740	model Movie {
741	  id    Int    @id     @default(autoincrement())
742	  name  String @unique
743	  seats Seat[]
744	}
745	```
746	
747	The following sample code finds the first available seat and assigns that seat to a user:
748	
749	```ts
750	const movieName = "Hidden Figures";
751	
752	// Find first available seat
753	const availableSeat = await prisma.seat.findFirst({
754	  where: {
755	    movie: {
756	      name: movieName,
757	    },
758	    claimedBy: null,
759	  },
760	});
761	
762	// Throw an error if no seats are available
763	if (!availableSeat) {
764	  throw new Error(`Oh no! ${movieName} is all booked.`);
765	}
766	
767	// Claim the seat
768	await prisma.seat.update({
769	  data: {
770	    claimedBy: userId,
771	  },
772	  where: {
773	    id: availableSeat.id,
774	  },
775	});
776	```
777	
778	However, this code suffers from the "double-booking problem" - it is possible for two people to book the same seats:
779	
780	1. Seat 3A returned to Sorcha (`findFirst`)
781	2. Seat 3A returned to Ellen (`findFirst`)
782	3. Seat 3A claimed by Sorcha (`update`)
783	4. Seat 3A claimed by Ellen (`update` - overwrites Sorcha's claim)
784	
785	Even though Sorcha has successfully booked the seat, the system ultimately stores Ellen's claim. To solve this problem with optimistic concurrency control, add a `version` field to the seat:
786	
787	```prisma highlight=7;normal
788	model Seat {
789	  id        Int   @id @default(autoincrement())
790	  userId    Int?
791	  claimedBy User? @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
792	  movieId   Int
793	  movie     Movie @relation(fields: [movieId], references: [id])
794	  version   Int // [!code highlight]
795	}
796	```
797	
798	Next, adjust the code to check the `version` field before updating:
799	
800	```ts highlight=19-38;normal
801	const userEmail = "alice@prisma.io";
802	const movieName = "Hidden Figures";
803	
804	// Find the first available seat
805	// availableSeat.version might be 0
806	const availableSeat = await client.seat.findFirst({
807	  where: {
808	    Movie: {
809	      name: movieName,
810	    },
811	    claimedBy: null,
812	  },
813	});
814	
815	if (!availableSeat) {
816	  throw new Error(`Oh no! ${movieName} is all booked.`);
817	}
818	
819	// Only mark the seat as claimed if the availableSeat.version // [!code highlight]
820	// matches the version we're updating. Additionally, increment the // [!code highlight]
821	// version when we perform this update so all other clients trying // [!code highlight]
822	// to book this same seat will have an outdated version. // [!code highlight]
823	const seats = await client.seat.updateMany({
824	  // [!code highlight]
825	  data: {
826	    // [!code highlight]
827	    claimedBy: userEmail, // [!code highlight]
828	    version: {
829	      // [!code highlight]
830	      increment: 1, // [!code highlight]
831	    }, // [!code highlight]
832	  }, // [!code highlight]
833	  where: {
834	    // [!code highlight]
835	    id: availableSeat.id, // [!code highlight]
836	    version: availableSeat.version, // This version field is the key; only claim seat if in-memory version matches database version, indicating that the field has not been updated // [!code highlight]
837	  }, // [!code highlight]
838	}); // [!code highlight]
839	
840	if (seats.count === 0) {
841	  // [!code highlight]
842	  throw new Error(`That seat is already booked! Please try again.`); // [!code highlight]
843	} // [!code highlight]
844	```
845	
846	It is now impossible for two people to book the same seat:
847	
848	1. Seat 3A returned to Sorcha (`version` is 0)
849	2. Seat 3A returned to Ellen (`version` is 0)
850	3. Seat 3A claimed by Sorcha (`version` is incremented to 1, booking succeeds)
851	4. Seat 3A claimed by Ellen (in-memory `version` (0) does not match database `version` (1) - booking does not succeed)
852	
853	### Interactive transactions
854	
855	If you have an existing application, it can be a significant undertaking to refactor your application to use optimistic concurrency control. Interactive Transactions offers a useful escape hatch for cases like this.
856	
857	To create an interactive transaction, pass an async function into [$transaction](#transaction-api).
858	
859	The first argument passed into this async function is an instance of the Prisma Client. Below, we will call this instance `tx`. Any Prisma Client call invoked on this `tx` instance is encapsulated into the transaction.
860	
861	In the example below, Alice and Bob each have $100 in their account. If they try to send more money than they have, the transfer is rejected.
862	
863	The expected outcome would be for Alice to make 1 transfer for $100 and the other transfer would be rejected. This would result in Alice having $0 and Bob having $200.
864	
865	```ts
866	import { PrismaClient } from "../prisma/generated/client";
867	const prisma = new PrismaClient();
868	
869	async function transfer(from: string, to: string, amount: number) {
870	  return await prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
871	    // 1. Decrement amount from the sender.
872	    const sender = await tx.account.update({
873	      data: {
874	        balance: {
875	          decrement: amount,
876	        },
877	      },
878	      where: {
879	        email: from,
880	      },
881	    });
882	
883	    // 2. Verify that the sender's balance didn't go below zero.
884	    if (sender.balance < 0) {
885	      throw new Error(`${from} doesn't have enough to send ${amount}`);
886	    }
887	
888	    // 3. Increment the recipient's balance by amount
889	    const recipient = tx.account.update({
890	      data: {
891	        balance: {
892	          increment: amount,
893	        },
894	      },
895	      where: {
896	        email: to,
897	      },
898	    });
899	
900	    return recipient;
901	  });
902	}
903	
904	async function main() {
905	  // This transfer is successful
906	  await transfer("alice@prisma.io", "bob@prisma.io", 100);
907	  // This transfer fails because Alice doesn't have enough funds in her account
908	  await transfer("alice@prisma.io", "bob@prisma.io", 100);
909	}
910	
911	main();
912	```
913	
914	In the example above, both `update` queries run within a database transaction. When the application reaches the end of the function, the transaction is **committed** to the database.
915	
916	If the application encounters an error along the way, the async function will throw an exception and automatically **rollback** the transaction.
917	
918	You can learn more about interactive transactions in this [section](#interactive-transactions).
919	
920	:::warning
921	
922	**Use interactive transactions with caution**. Keeping transactions
923	open for a long time hurts database performance and can even cause deadlocks.
924	Try to avoid performing network requests and executing slow queries inside your
925	transaction functions. We recommend you get in and out as quick as possible!
926	
927	:::
928	
929	## Conclusion
930	
931	Prisma Client supports multiple ways of handling transactions, either directly through the API or by supporting your ability to introduce optimistic concurrency control and idempotency into your application. If you feel like you have use cases in your application that are not covered by any of the suggested options, please open a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/prisma/prisma/issues/new/choose) to start a discussion.
932

Good, thanks for asking! For your case, the two writes are **independent** (each just sets its own `order` value), so use `$transaction([])` with two `update` calls:

```ts
await prisma.$transaction([
  prisma.todoGroup.update({ where: { id: groupAId }, data: { order: 2 } }),
  prisma.todoGroup.update({ where: { id: groupBId }, data: { order: 1 } }),
]);
```

This runs both updates atomically — either both succeed or neither does.

Source: `apps/docs/content/docs/orm/v7/prisma-client/queries/transactions.mdx`, sections "Independent writes" and "Using `$transaction([])` for independent writes" (lines 310–333).
